final_answer:
IMPORTANT LIMITATION: every primary-source fetch (eCFR, US Code, Federal Register, Cornell, congress.gov, govinfo, DOJ) was blocked by the network proxy, so no authority was verified under the citation firewall. The answer below is from background knowledge plus one search-result summary, and is not cited as verified support.

Bottom line: the husband's route is a motion to reopen with the immigration court to rescind the in absentia order for lack of notice. Only after rescission can he seek to revive the I-130/I-485. This is a strong and cheap route if he never received a valid NTA.

1. Immigration court filing. File a motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia order under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii), with the Immigration Court that entered the order. The basis is that he did not receive notice of the hearing as required by INA 239(a)(1) or (2). The statute and regulation set no deadline for a lack-of-notice motion, so the motion is timely on April 1, 2026 even though the order issued August 1, 2025. The 180-day deadline applies only to the exceptional-circumstances ground in 240(b)(5)(C)(i). Filing the motion automatically stays removal until the court rules (INA 240(b)(5)(C)). Include a Form EOIR-33/IC (change of address) and EOIR-28 if represented, a cover page, a proposed order, proof of service on DHS/ICE OPLA, and the other items the Immigration Court Practice Manual requires. Attach the husband's declaration (or an affidavit) saying that he never lived at or received mail at the address USCIS used and never gave it to anyone. Also attach evidence of his real address: the I-130/I-485 filing, lease, and so on. Attach the USCIS filings showing the correct address, the RFE mailed to the wrong address, and the NTA and hearing notice. If the NTA was sent only by mail to an address he never provided, then notice was defective. Add the argument that the NTA never gave the time and place (Pereira v. Sessions, Niz-Chavez v. Garland) if the NTA was deficient. Note that a presumption of delivery applies to regular mail and is weaker where the address itself was wrong. Also note the possible argument that the INA 239(a)(2)(A) obligation to provide a current address was never triggered if he never received a valid NTA. He may also ask the court to terminate or continue so that he can pursue relief. Next steps after rescission: the court resets proceedings with a proper NTA, and he can apply for adjustment of status in court as a defense to removal (the I-485 can be renewed before the IJ, with a new I-130 as a basis, as he is an immediate relative).

2. Fees. The motion to reopen under 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) for lack of notice is, to my understanding, fee-exempt, both under the 8 CFR 1003.24 exemption for such motions and under the H.R. 1 (Pub. L. 119-21) EOIR fee provisions. A search-result summary said the H.R. 1 fee does not apply to a motion filed under 240(b)(5)(C)(ii). I could not verify the statute or rules directly. By contrast, a motion based on exceptional circumstances under (C)(i) carries the $145 motion fee plus the H.R. 1 fee (about $900, reported as $920 after inflation adjustment, about $1,065 total). H.R. 1 fees cannot be waived on the ordinary fee-waiver route. Confirm current amounts on the EOIR fee schedule before filing; if the court finds notice was proper, a (C)(i) motion would be untimely anyway. A cautious practitioner may prepare a request in the alternative.

3. Contesting the I-130/I-485 denials. The USCIS denials were issued on December 5, 2023 and January 15, 2024. Deadlines have long passed: an appeal of the I-130 denial to the BIA (Form I-290B) is due within 30 days (33 if mailed), and a motion to reopen or reconsider with USCIS (8 CFR 103.5) is due within the same 30 days. There is no appeal of a denied I-485 outside removal proceedings. Possible recourse: (a) ask USCIS to reopen on its own motion (8 CFR 103.5(a)(5)) on the ground that it sent the RFE and denial to the wrong address (this is discretionary), and (b) the more practical path is to file a new I-130 (and, once in proceedings, to renew the I-485 before the IJ). Because the denial was a failure to respond to an RFE, there is no adjudicated merits finding against the marriage. Be aware that the final removal order may foreclose a new USCIS I-485 until the order is rescinded, and that an adjustment applicant who entered on a B-2 and married within weeks faces a possible misrepresentation (INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i)) inquiry from the 90-day guideline. Immediate-relative status and 245(a) eligibility (inspected and admitted) remain available since he was admitted on a B-2; unlawful status after June 1, 2023 does not bar an immediate relative under 245(c).

4. If the motion is denied: appeal to the BIA (Form EOIR-26, 30 days, with fee) and petition for review to the circuit court within 30 days.

Caveat: all of the above must be checked against current text of the statute, regulations, and fee rules, which I could not access.
